item.title: Why Your Brain Needs Nature
item.description:
Environment

Why Your Brain Needs Nature

The emerging science of how our surroundings shape attention, stress, and cognition.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Being in nature may benefit our physiology, including autonomic and stress responses.
  • Nature may support brain functions, including attention, mood, and cognition.
  • Nature’s “soft fascination” may give our constantly directed attention a chance to recover.
  • Environmental neuroscience studies how our surroundings influence the brain.

We have all experienced it: stress at work. You are staring at your computer, deadlines mounting, stuck on a project. Taking a walk seems like a waste of time, but you decide to go outside anyway. Maybe there is a small park near your office or home. You breathe in the air, look at the sky and clouds, and notice some greenery; trees, grass, perhaps a few flowers. You hear a bird in the distance and feel the wind against your face.

And suddenly, you feel lighter. Your mood lifts. A random idea connects. You remember a coworker from a previous project whom you can ask for help.

Or, even better, you go for a hike on the weekend. The crisp air, the smell of trees, the chirping of birds, the sound of a stream all feel refreshing. Your worries begin to recede.

And the restorative effect lasts even after you come home and turn the computer back on. Sure, your legs are sore and your muscles a little tired, but mentally, you feel refreshed, ready to face the task that seemed so daunting before.

The Emerging Field of Environmental Neuroscience

Marc G. Berman, author of Nature and the Mind, studied this exact effect of nature on our brain in a scientific fashion.

In a now-classic experiment, participants first completed a cognitive task called the backward digit span, which requires them to listen to a series of numbers and repeat them in reverse order. Then, they took a walk outside for about an hour. One group walked in the Arboretum, in a trail following a river through the evergreeens, and the other, in the busy part of the town, navigating intersections along the commercial storefronts. When they returned, they repeated the same test. The participants who walked in nature significantly improved their scores, but those who did the urban walk did not.

Later, the researchers switched the routes, so the same people served as their own controls and the result was the same: nature walk improved attention and memory, but urban walk did not. The walking was similar. The people were the same. What changed was the environment.

The researchers suggested that nature captures our attention gently, without demanding it. Urban environments, in contrast, are filled with stimulation that demands our attention, such as traffic, signs, people, and potential hazards. Nature, they suggested, gives our directed attention a chance to recover.

Berman is now considered to be one of the leaders of an emerging field, environmental neuroscience, which studies how features of our environment influence the brain, including our attention, cognition, mood and stress. In retrospect, this seems obvious. Our brain is the interface between our inner world and the world outside us. Why wouldn't the environment in which it operates matter?

Environmental Neuroscience Taps Traditions Like Shinrin-Yoku (Forest Medicine)

The idea that nature can help our health is not new. Research from another tradition suggests that nature's effects may extend beyond cognition into the body itself.

In Japan, interest in the health effects of shinrin-yoku, or “forest bathing,” has grown, alongside an emerging discipline known as “forest medicine.” Shinrin means “forest” in Japanese, and yoku means “bath.” It is specifically noted that Shinrin-yoku is not exercise, or hiking. Rather, it is the act of being in nature, bathing in the forest atmosphere and connecting with it through our multisensory system of sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch.

Studies have associated forest exposure with lower cortisol levels, changes in autonomic measures, improvements in mood, and changes in measures of immune function.

One intriguing hypothesis involves phytoncides, volatile organic compounds released by trees. Laboratory and small human studies suggest that these compounds may contribute to some of the physiological effects associated with forest exposure, including changes in natural killer cell activity. But they are unlikely to explain the whole story.

Nature's "sofr fascination" maybe restorative to our brain
Source: Michiko Bruno

Why Nature Helps our Brain

Recent studies using tools such as functional MRI and EEG are beginning to show that natural and urban environments engage the brain differently, including networks involved in attention, stress, emotion, and self-referential thought.

According to Attention restoration theory (ART), “attention” is a finite resource, that can be depleted by constant stimulation.

Modern life constantly demands directed attention: ignore the notification, answer the email, switch between windows, remember the deadline at work—while also scheduling the dentist appointment, arranging the car safety check, and figuring out the family vacation.

Our attention rarely gets to be off duty. Nature captures attention differently. A cloud moving, leaves rustling, water flowing, birds calling—these attract us without demanding that we concentrate on them.

This gentle capture of attention has been described as “soft fascination”: interesting enough to engage us, but not so demanding that it taxes our directed attention. This may give our attentional resources an opportunity to recover.

In short, looking at trees may restore attention when scrolling through something entertaining on your phone does not.

One of the intriguing ideas that researchers have begun to ask is whether some of nature’s restorative qualities lie in visual geometry. Built environments are often dominated by straight lines, sharp edges, and regular geometry. Natural environments tend to contain more curves, irregularity, and complex patterns. Nature also tends to contain repeating patterns at different scales: the branching of a tree, the veins of a leaf, the irregular edge of a coastline, what may be called as “fractal.” patterns.

Studies suggest that people generally prefer natural images, and viewing them can improve mood. But preference alone does not appear to explain nature's cognitive benefits. In Berman's studies, participants did not necessarily have to enjoy their nature walk more to show improvement in cognitive performance.

nature's fractal pattern is easy on your attention
Source: Michiko Bruno

In other words, nature's cognitive benefits may involve more than simply enjoying what we see. Something about how the brain processes natural environments may itself matter.

***

So the next time you are staring at your computer, stuck on a problem, going for a walk may not be procrastination. It may be exactly what your brain needs.

Neuroscience has historically spent far more time studying what happens inside the brain. Environmental neuroscience is beginning to change that. If our surroundings influence attention, stress, mood, and cognition, then the environments we build are not simply backgrounds. They are part of the biological conditions in which our brains function.

Perhaps brain health begins not only with what we do to our brains, but with the worlds we ask our brains to live in.

item.title: Leadership Requires Composure in the Pocket
item.description:
Leadership

Leadership Requires Composure in the Pocket

The pocket is where leadership becomes reactivity or thought.

Posted August 17, 2026

Source: Memento Media/Unsplash

Beneath the obvious pressures a leader faces in the work itself, there are undercurrents involving emotional fields and self-differentiation, systemic psychological dynamics, that distort decision-making by leaders who otherwise consider themselves rational. In many organizations, the leader who moves first under pressure is credited with decisiveness, while the leader who slows the pace is suspected of hesitation or obstructionism. Over time, this trains systems to reward speed even when what is being rewarded is often reactivity.

Murray Bowen’s language is useful here. Bowen defined "differentiation of self" as variation in people’s capacity to remain calm and clear‑headed under relational pressure — i.e., connected to others without being governed by the emotional field. Differentiation describes the capacity to remain in contact with others without surrendering the organizing function of one’s own thinking. That capacity is mostly built outside of moments that appear decisive.

A quarterback metaphor may help convey the experience, though in football the interval is brief, measured in seconds, whereas in leadership it may extend over minutes, days, or even months. The pocket is a state that becomes more precarious the longer it is held. Everything in the situation converges on its collapse. The discipline lies in remaining there long enough for the play to develop and then acting from one’s own thinking rather than from the surrounding movement. When that discipline fails, what appears to be initiative is often just a reaction to pressure.

A CEO I worked for emailed staff ahead of visiting my site, noting that he was an introvert and socially reserved. He invited others to initiate conversation with him. This may be close to what Bowen meant by defining a self without imposing it. Much of leadership language softens that idea into authenticity or encourages its opposite under the label of influence, but it is more complex and nuanced than either and involves a three-dimensionality that involves self-awareness, empathy, and proactive communication.

Groups regulate themselves through discomfort. Anxiety moves quickly through an organization, attaching to decisions that can carry it and to people who are susceptible to carrying it. Many of the familiar patterns—triangulation, over-functioning, a sense of urgency treated as necessity—are ways of redistributing that load. A leader who can absorb some measure of it without reacting slows the system enough to allow a more accurate reading of what is at stake, which is a form of discernment.

Source: Dave Adamson/Unsplash

The risk is that restraint is misinterpreted as passivity or indecision and gradually abandoned. The leader begins to anticipate the group’s expectations and respond preemptively to internally felt pressure and anxiety. Systems stabilize around such accommodation. It is difficult to reverse because it works, at least in the narrow sense of reducing visible friction. It is often expedient but not wise.

There is no technique that substitutes for the capacity to remain there, organized around one’s own thinking, under the pressure inherent to the emotional field of the pocket. Understanding one’s position in a family or organizational system, noticing predictable moves under strain, and practicing small acts of differentiation in low-stakes settings build a reserve of steadiness that can be drawn upon later.

If the metaphor of a quarterback in the pocket is useful, it is because it returns attention to timing and urgency. There are points in professional exchanges where pressures from a blitzing emotional field begin to accelerate, and, under those conditions, thinking tends to narrow as people shift to faster, more simplified judgments. The impulse is to match that energy. Occasionally that is appropriate. Often it is not. Remaining long enough for thinking to reassert itself is a critical decision about the terms on which any action will be carried out. In those moments, the pressure is not only to decide, but to stay put long enough to separate the actual problem from the pressure being routed through it.

The difference shows up most clearly over time. Leaders who habitually take their cues from the surrounding energy tend to produce decisions that fit the moment and age poorly. For leaders who can hold their position in the midst of that energy, a path for action tends to take shape. This approach makes space, however briefly, for decisions that are not simply the product of the loudest forces present.

Source: Keith Johnston/Unsplash

In practice, this means accepting that much of what passes for leadership effectiveness is situational and will fluctuate with the system's level of anxiety. It also means refusing to anchor one's own functioning to that fluctuation. The pocket, if it is more than a metaphor, is simply a span of time in which a person remains organized around their own thinking while in full contact with others who are not. It does not last. Which means it comes down to whether the leader has the discipline of composure to bear the quiet strain of remaining there while the field presses in.
